# Database Transaction Recovery After Power Failure

A power failure is the canonical "crash" scenario that every transactional database must survive. When the machine loses power, everything in volatile memory — the buffer pool, the log tail, in-flight locks, and the state of partially executed transactions — vanishes instantly. Yet the durability guarantee of ACID (the "D") promises that any transaction that *committed* before the crash is still there afterward, and the atomicity guarantee (the "A") promises that any transaction that was *not* committed leaves no trace. # How a Compiler Detects and Optimizes Repeated Expressions

Repeated expressions—computing the same value more than once—are among the most common sources of wasted work in programs. Compilers attack this problem with a family of techniques collectively called **redundancy elimination**, of which **common subexpression elimination (CSE)** is the canonical example. This article explains how a compiler *detects* repeated expressions, how it *optimizes* them, walks through concrete worked examples at several levels (local, global, and partial redundancy), and discusses the limitations that keep these optimizations from being universally applicable.

# TCP Congestion Control: Adaptation to Changing Bandwidth

TCP congestion control is the set of algorithms that governs how aggressively a sender injects packets into the network. Its central challenge is that the network's available bandwidth is unknown, time-varying, and shared with other flows. TCP must therefore *discover* capacity empirically—probing upward until loss or delay signals congestion, then backing off—while remaining fair to competing flows and efficient enough to use the link. This essay explains the mechanisms by which TCP adapts to changing bandwidth, works through concrete numerical examples, and discusses the limitations of the approach.
